CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and swelling following motor vehicle accident.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male presenting for a second opinion regarding a hyperextension injury to his right index finger sustained in March 2026 during a motor vehicle accident when his car was rear-ended multiple times. The patient reports that the impact caused him to stretch out his right index finger, which has been painful and swollen since the injury. He states he cannot make a fist and describes the pain as sometimes unbearable, even while driving. He has been experiencing symptoms for approximately three months. The patient was previously seen at Point May Orthopedics and underwent physical therapy, followed by MRI imaging. He was offered a steroid injection but initially declined due to prior adverse reaction to dexamethasone causing tachycardia. He reports conflicting information from his previous providers regarding treatment recommendations and feels he has not been receiving adequate medical care. An MRI obtained on 4/24/2026 showed focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of the right flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon, and fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint and the MCP joint capsule were intact, and extensor tendons were deemed intact.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Denies other systemic complaints.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history noted other than adverse reactions to steroids.

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication (specific agent not documented).

ALLERGIES
Dexamethasone (causes tachycardia).
Methylprednisolone (causes itching).

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as an X-ray technician and is right-handed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no distress. Vital signs stable with regular rate and rhythm; 2+ radial pulse.
Hand: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Tenderness to palpation at the MCP joint. Mild numbness noted. Patient reports pain with active flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint. Able to make a fist. Collateral ligaments intact. Extensors intact. X-rays today show no bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits on the right hand, no soft tissue shadows of concern, and no arthritis.

RESULTS
X-rays of the right hand (4 views): No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no arthritis.
MRI (4/24/2026): Focal soft tissue swelling over right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of right FDS tendon, fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around FDP and FDS tendons, radial and ulnar collateral ligaments intact, MCP joint capsule intact, extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger with partial-thickness tear of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon.

Plan:
1. Steroid injection: Attempted right trigger finger injection with betamethasone (1 cc) and lidocaine (0.5 cc). Patient had a dramatic and violent painful reaction to needle introduction on first attempt with hand contortions and concerns for secondary needle stick. Second attempt was made with same medication and technique. Small palmar vein bleeding occurred, which was cleaned and bandaged. Patient reassured that no harm was done to finger.
2. Medications: Ibuprofen as needed; ice this evening.
3. Physical therapy: Outpatient occupational therapy once weekly for six weeks with goals of full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. Patient counseled on importance of active movement of finger to prevent stiffness and maximize therapeutic benefit of steroid injection.
4. Patient educated that steroid effect typically begins in 3-5 days with continued improvement over the next couple of weeks.
5. Assured that it is safe to drive.
6. Follow-up as needed; repeat steroid injection may be necessary.
